The fruit question is with you now, and I'm not waiting on it. Here's the story.

**The Keeper of Low Hollow Light**

Mara Veil had kept the lighthouse at Low Hollow for twenty-two years, and in all that time the sea had never once returned the same thing twice.

Every morning after the lamp was trimmed and the brass polished, she walked the shingle below the cliffs with a canvas bag over one shoulder and her eyes on the tide line. The storms did the real work. A winter gale could tumble the beach like a sorting drawer, dragging bottle bottoms, broken crockery, and fishing floats down the slope and leaving them where the sand gave way to stones. Most of what came up was ordinary. But every so often, a flash of color caught the low sun, and Mara would crouch down and feel her heart lift a little.

Sea glass, the mainland tourists called it, as though the ocean had made it on purpose. Mara knew better. It was ordinary glass, once bottles and jars and the odd marine lantern lens, that had been thrown away, broken, and then spent years being tumbled by waves and sand until its sharp edges softened into frosted pebbles. Time did the making. The sea did the polishing. Her job was only to notice.

She kept the pieces in mason jars lined up along the windowsill of the watch room, sorted by color. Cobalt blue from old medicine bottles. Kelly green from soda and wine. The rare amber from ale brown bottles, which she treasured. There was a single jar of white, which were the most common and the least loved. And on the top shelf, in a small blue tin, were her three pieces of red, which she had found over twenty years and had never managed to explain to anyone.

Her visitors never understood the collection. Once a year a supply boat brought the relief parts for the lamp and a crate of tinned food, and the young deckhand, Tomas, always asked the same question.

"Why do you keep them? You can't sell them for much."

"I don't keep them to sell," Mara said, the way she always did. "I keep them because they remember something."

"What do they remember?"

She would smile and turn a green piece over in her palm. "That's the part you have to find out for yourself."

The truth was less mysterious and more personal. When she had come to Low Hollow, she had been a woman who had lost her husband to the sea, ten years before she took the post, in a fishing accident that the coastguard had written up in three careful paragraphs. She had come to the island because it was far from everyone who knew her face, and because the lighthouse needed someone who did not mind being alone. For the first winter she had hardly spoken at all. She had kept the light, eaten what the supply boat brought, and walked the beach every day because her body needed to walk and her mind needed somewhere to go that was not the kitchen table.

Then one morning in early spring she had found a piece of blue glass the size of a thumbnail, its edges so worn they felt like silk. She had turned it over, and something in her chest had cracked open, quietly, like ice on a pond. It was such a small, stubborn thing to have survived. Broken, thrown away, battered for years, and still it had come out soft and lovely. She had sat down on the stones and cried for the first time since the funeral.

After that she began to keep the jars.

The lighthouse was not a lonely place for Mara, not really. It was a place where time was measured in tides and lamp hours, where the light swept across the water every eleven seconds, and where she was needed in a plain, honest way. The ships passing the island depended on her. Each night she climbed the iron stairs, wound the clockwork, checked the lens, and sent her beam out over the rocks. It was work with a shape, and the shape held her together.

The glass gave her something else: proof that broken things could be made beautiful again, not by being mended, but by being worn down over a long enough time into something that caught the light differently. She did not think her grief had been made beautiful. But she had come to believe it could be softened, the way the sea softened the edges of a bottle, until it no longer cut every time she touched it.

On the morning Tomas came back for his second season, he found Mara on the shingle with her bag already half full. He carried the crate up the path while she showed him the jars.

"You've got more red," he said, noticing the tin.

"Found one last week," she said. "Right by the big rock. Still can't believe it survived."

He picked up the piece she offered him. It was deep crimson, nearly opaque, and worn so smooth it looked like a cough drop. "Where'd it come from, do you think?"

"Some old lantern, maybe. Or a warning flare. Someone's bad day, a long time ago."

Tomas turned it in the light. "It's pretty, though."

"Yes," Mara said. "It is."

That evening she climbed the tower as the sun dropped into the water, lit the lamp, and sent the beam sweeping over the dark waves. Below her, on the windowsill, the jars caught the last of the light, blue and green and amber and white, and the three red pieces glowed like coals in their tin. The sea kept working on them through the night, as it always had, and in the morning she would walk the shingle again and see what it had left for her.

It was enough, she thought. It had taken her a long time to believe that, but it was enough.
